lesson.title: Wireshark: Making the Invisible Network Visible
lesson.summary: Wireshark is a graphical packet analyzer that captures live network traffic and decodes every field of every packet, turning invisible network behavior into something you can actually read.
lesson.body:
A packet leaves your computer, crosses a switch, maybe a router or two, and arrives at its destination in a few milliseconds. Almost none of that is visible from an application. When a web page hangs or a video call drops, the application layer only tells you the symptom: the page did not load, the call disconnected. To find out why, you need to look at the actual packets moving across the wire, and that is exactly what Wireshark is for.

Wireshark is a graphical tool that captures packets from a network interface and decodes them layer by layer: Ethernet header, IP header, TCP or UDP header, and then whatever application-layer protocol sits on top, such as HTTP, DNS, or TLS. Because it understands the structure of a packet, it does not just show you raw bytes, it shows you labeled fields you can read directly, like source port, sequence number, or HTTP status code. This only makes sense once you understand what a packet actually is: a unit of data wrapped in headers from multiple layers, each header added by a different layer of the network stack. Wireshark's whole value is that it unwraps those headers for you instead of leaving you to decode hex by hand.

Consider a concrete troubleshooting scenario. A web application intermittently times out for users, but only sometimes, and only for some requests. You start a Wireshark capture on the client machine, reproduce the problem, and stop the capture. Instead of scrolling through thousands of packets, you apply a display filter like tcp.port == 443 to isolate the relevant connection, then look for warning signs Wireshark highlights automatically: TCP retransmissions (the same segment sent more than once, meaning the receiver never acknowledged it), duplicate ACKs (a sign of packet loss upstream), or a TCP RST packet abruptly tearing down the connection. If the handshake itself, the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange, takes an unusually long time before the first data flows, that points to network latency rather than the application. If the connection completes fine but then stalls for seconds before a response, that points to the server being slow, not the network. Wireshark's Follow TCP Stream feature lets you reconstruct the entire conversation as a human-readable sequence, which is often the fastest way to confirm whether the client or the server caused the delay.

It is worth being clear about what Wireshark can and cannot see. If the traffic is encrypted with TLS, which most application-layer traffic is today, Wireshark can still show you the TCP behavior, the handshake timing, and the unencrypted TLS handshake metadata, but not the HTTP request or response contents unless you have separately provided the session keys. This is not a limitation of the tool, it is by design: encryption is supposed to keep contents private from anyone capturing the traffic, including you. Understanding this boundary is part of using Wireshark correctly rather than assuming it can decode anything.
